subject: gold metal
title: Gold Hit 19,000 Kelvin, Hotter Than the Sun, and Didn't Melt

scenes.text: Scientists heated gold hotter than the Sun. It didn't melt.
Gold normally melts at about a thousand degrees Celsius.
In 2025, a Stanford lab hit a thin gold film with a laser, reaching nineteen thousand kelvin. Fourteen times its melting point.
Physicists thought no solid could survive past three times its melting point.
So why didn't it melt? The heat arrived in under a trillionth of a second, too fast for the atoms to spread apart.
Hotter than the Sun's surface, and still solid.

description:
Scientists heated gold to about 19,000 kelvin (33,740 F), more than 14 times its melting point, and it stayed solid.
The SLAC team (Nature, 2025) heated a 50-nanometer gold film with a 45-femtosecond laser pulse, so fast the metal had no time to expand. A 1980s theory, the entropy catastrophe, said solids could not survive past about three times their melting point.
What should scientists try to overheat next?
first_comment: Bonus: the whole blast lasted 45 quadrillionths of a second. What would you want to see heated like this?
